Our examination kept us there until dark, when we left. On the way home, my companion stopped briefly at the office of a daily newspaper.

I have said that my friend had many whims, and that je les ménageais—a phrase with no exact English equivalent. His present whim was to refuse any discussion of the murder until about noon the following day. Then he suddenly asked whether I had noticed anything peculiar at the scene of the crime.

Something in the way he stressed the word ‘peculiar’ made me shudder, though I could not say why.

‘No, nothing peculiar,’ I answered; ‘nothing, at least, beyond what we both read in the newspaper.’

‘The Gazette,’ he replied, ‘has failed, I fear, to grasp the unusual horror of the affair. But put aside that paper's pointless opinions. It seems to me that people think this mystery impossible to solve for the very reason they should think it easy: its bizarre details. The police are baffled by the apparent lack of motive—not for the murder itself, but for its extraordinary brutality. They cannot explain the voices heard arguing, either, when the only person found upstairs was the murdered Mademoiselle L'Espanaye, and nobody could have escaped without being seen by the people coming up. The room's terrible disorder; the corpse pushed headfirst up the chimney; the dreadful mutilation of the old woman's body—these facts, along with those already mentioned and others I need not describe, have left the official investigators helpless, defeating the sharp judgment they boast of. They have made the serious but common mistake of confusing what is unusual with what is difficult to understand. Yet these departures from the ordinary are precisely what enable reason, if anything can, to find its way toward the truth. In an investigation like ours, the question should be less “What happened?” than “What happened that has never happened before?” In fact, the more impossible the police find this mystery, the easier I shall find—or have already found—its solution.’

I stared at him in silent amazement.

‘I am now waiting,’ he continued, looking toward our apartment door, ‘I am now waiting for someone who, though perhaps not responsible for carrying out these butcheries, must have been involved in them to some degree.’

I drew alongside a stout fellow with a plump, cheerful face, intending to be pleasant and gather a few more scraps of information; but we had scarcely struck up an acquaintance when he began, eagerly and clumsily, to work his way, in the time-honored fashion, toward that same ancient anecdote—the one Sir Dinadan related when I fell into trouble with Sir Sagramor and received his challenge on its account. I made my excuses and fell back to the tail of the procession, heavy-hearted, ready to depart this troubled life, this valley of tears, this brief day of interrupted repose, of cloud and tempest, of tiresome struggle and unvarying defeat; yet recoiling from the change when I recalled the length of eternity, and the numbers who had gone there knowing that anecdote.

Early that afternoon we came up with another procession of pilgrims; but this one had no merriment, no jests, no laughter, no sportive behavior, nor any joyful lightheadedness of either youth or age. Yet both were present, age and youth alike: grey old men and women, vigorous men and women in middle life, young husbands and wives, small boys and girls, and three nursing babies. Even the children never smiled; every face among these fifty people was downcast, wearing that fixed look of hopelessness born of prolonged, bitter trials and an ancient familiarity with despair. They were slaves. Chains ran from the fetters at their feet and the manacles at their wrists to a belt of sole-leather around each waist; and everyone except the children was further joined in a line, six feet apart, by one chain running from collar to collar throughout the file. They traveled on foot, and had marched three hundred miles in eighteen days, living on the cheapest scraps of food, grudgingly portioned out. Every night they had slept in these chains, huddled like pigs. A few wretched rags hung upon their bodies, but they could hardly be called clothed. Their irons had rubbed the skin off their ankles, leaving sores that were ulcerated and crawling with worms. Their bare feet were lacerated, and every one of them limped. These unfortunate people had numbered a hundred originally, but nearly half had been sold along the road. The dealer responsible for them rode horseback and held a whip with a short handle and a long, weighty lash, split at its end into several knotted tails. Whenever someone faltered with fatigue and pain, he slashed their shoulders with it and brought them upright. He uttered no word; the whip made his wishes plain enough.

Recent reports from Rotterdam suggest that the city is in a considerable ferment of philosophical excitement. Phenomena have indeed occurred there so wholly unforeseen—so entirely unprecedented—so thoroughly opposed to established notions—that I cannot doubt that by this time all Europe is in uproar, all physics in turmoil, and reason and astronomy at each other's throats.

It seems that on the —— day of —— (I cannot be certain of the date), an immense gathering, for reasons not particularly recorded, had collected in the great Exchange square of the prosperous city of Rotterdam. The weather was warm—exceptionally warm for the season—and scarcely a breath stirred; the crowd therefore took no offense at the occasional friendly sprinklings of brief rain that descended from the great white clouds irregularly dappling the blue arch of heaven. Toward noon, however, a slight yet noticeable disturbance passed through the assembly. Ten thousand tongues began to clatter; a moment later, ten thousand faces turned skyward, ten thousand pipes dropped together from the corners of ten thousand mouths, and a cry comparable only to Niagara's roar rang long, loud, and fiercely throughout the neighborhood of Rotterdam.

The source of this commotion soon grew plain enough. From behind the enormous bulk of one of the sharply outlined clouds just described, something strange, composite, and apparently substantial could be seen emerging slowly into a clear patch of blue. Its shape was so singular, its construction so capricious, that the multitude of sturdy citizens gaping below could neither understand it in the least nor sufficiently admire it. What might it be? In the name of every vrow and devil in Rotterdam, what could it possibly signify? Nobody knew; nobody could guess; nobody—not even the burgomaster, Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk—possessed the slightest clue to the mystery. Since no more sensible course presented itself, every man carefully restored his pipe to the corner of his mouth and, turning his right eye upward toward the apparition, puffed, paused, waddled about, and grunted meaningfully; then waddled back, grunted, paused, and at last—puffed once more.

Meanwhile, the object of all this curiosity, and occasion of all this smoke, descended lower and lower toward the worthy city. Within a few minutes it had approached closely enough for its form to be clearly distinguished. It seemed to be—yes! beyond question it was a kind of balloon; yet certainly no balloon of this description had ever before appeared in Rotterdam.
